worked_example.problem: On a map with scale {ratio(n)}, the road from the school to the market measures {cm} cm. How long is the real road?
steps: 1 cm on the map is {fmt(n)} cm on the ground.
{cm} cm on the map is {cm} × {fmt(n)} = {fmt(cm * n)} cm on the ground.
There are {fmt(factor('km', 'cm'))} cm in 1 km, so {fmt(cm * n)} cm = {fmt(realKm(cm, n))} km.

cards.idea: A globe has the true shape of the Earth but is small and hard to carry. A map is flat: it can show a small place in detail and fit in a bag.
example: To walk around Bamenda, take a map. To see the whole Earth’s shape, look at a globe.

check.prompt: Which is true about globes and maps?

right.text: A globe shows the true shape of the Earth.
A map can show a small area, such as a town, in detail.
A map is easy to fold and carry.

wrong.text: A globe is easier to carry than a map.
wrong.explain: A globe is round and bulky; a map can be folded.

wrong.text: A map is a model in the shape of a ball.
wrong.explain: That is a globe; a map is flat.

wrong.text: A globe can show every street of a town.
wrong.explain: A globe is too small for that; a large-scale map can show streets.

cards.idea: The marginal information around a map helps you read it: title, key, scale, north arrow and grid numbers.
example: The key tells you that a blue line is a river and a dashed line is a road.

cards.idea: A scale can be written in words (“1 cm represents 1 km”), as a ratio ({ratio(n)}), or drawn as a line marked in kilometres.
example: {ratio(n)} means 1 cm on the map is {fmt(n)} cm on the ground.

cards.idea: To find a real distance: measure in cm on the map, multiply by the scale number, and change cm to km.
example: {cm} cm on a {ratio(n)} map: {cm} × {fmt(n)} = {fmt(cm * n)} cm = {fmt(realKm(cm, n))} km.

check.prompt: On a map with scale {ratio(100000)}, 1 cm represents 1 km. Two villages are {cm} cm apart on the map. How far apart are they on the ground?

misconceptions.explain: That is in centimetres. Change it to kilometres.

solution: Each cm on this map is 1 km on the ground.

pick.why: The title tells you what place the map shows.
The key explains what each symbol and colour means.
The scale tells you how a distance on the map compares with the real distance.
The north arrow shows which way is north.
The grid numbers name the grid lines, to help you find places.

misconceptions.explain: Not that part. Read what each part of the marginal information does.

questions.prompt: A map has the scale {ratio(n)}. Two villages are {cm} cm apart on the map. How far apart are they on the ground?

misconceptions.explain: That is in metres. There are 100 000 cm in a kilometre, not 100.
That is in centimetres. Divide by 100 000 to get kilometres.

solution: 1 cm on the map = {fmt(n)} cm on the ground.

questions.prompt: On a map, 1 cm represents {k} km. Write this scale as a ratio.

misconceptions.explain: 1 km is 1000 metres, but the ratio must use the same unit on both sides: centimetres. 1 km = 100 000 cm.

solution: Both sides must be in cm: {k} km = {k} × {fmt(factor('km', 'cm'))} = {fmt(k * 100000)} cm.

pick.why: “1 cm represents 2 km” is a statement scale.
a line divided into kilometres is a linear scale.
“one centimetre to half a kilometre” is a statement scale.

misconceptions.explain: Not this kind. Words: statement. Numbers 1 : n: ratio. A line marked in km: linear scale.

questions.prompt: A road is {fmt(km)} km long. How long is it on a map with the scale {ratio(n)}?

misconceptions.explain: You multiplied by the scale. Going from the ground to the map, the distance gets smaller: divide.
That is the real distance in cm. Now divide by the scale number to get the map distance.
